s0.why: [1] calls it a steep conical landform of loose pyroclastic fragments such as ash or scoria built around a vent.

s1.why: [3] describes gas-charged lava blown into the air, breaking into fragments that solidify and fall, forming an often symmetrical cone with 30-40 degree slopes.

s2.why: [14] gives the gas loss, [16] the loose cinders too weak to support rising molten rock, [17] the denser lava and [18] the breakout along the bottom.

f1.why: [5] says tens to hundreds of meters tall.

f2.why: [27] calls Paricutin the most famous cinder cone, grown from a corn field in Mexico in 1943.

f3.why: [28] says eruptions continued nine years and built the cone to 424 meters; that is its height when eruptions stopped.

q1.why: [16] says lava rarely issues from the top since the cinders are too weak; [17]-[18] say the denser lava burrows out along the bottom, lifting cinders like corks.

q2.why: [8] says the material is glassy with bubbles frozen in as magma exploded into the air and cooled quickly; [3] gives the fragmenting in air.

q3.why: [35]-[36] say lower gravity and atmospheric pressure spread particles wider, with Martian cones more than twice as wide.

q4.why: [38] says strong prevailing winds pile more cinder on the downwind side; a west wind makes that the east side.

q5.why: [43]-[45] say a very low magma supply stops any eruption establishing plumbing, so each must find its own path.

q6.why: [6] distinguishes loose cinder cones from spatter cones made of agglomerated volcanic bombs.
